title: Seven Seconds of Now — Patient H.M., Clive Wearing & How Memory Stitches Time

teenKit.tldr: When a 1953 brain surgery accidentally deleted a young man's ability to form new memories, science finally learned that memory isn't just one big blob in the brain. Different biological parts handle past, present, and physical skills completely separately.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how our brains stitch time together reveals that your continuous sense of self is a delicate, biological illusion built by tiny structures deep inside your head.
keyTakeaways: Patient H.M.'s surgery proved that the medial temporal lobes are strictly required to lock new everyday facts and experiences into long-term storage.

Procedural memory—like learning physical skills—runs on a totally separate biological track from conscious factual memory, as shown by H.M. mastering the mirror-star drawing task without ever remembering practicing it.
Brain cells called 'time cells' in the hippocampus act like an internal metronome, firing in sequence to bridge the gaps between conscious moments and build our perception of a timeline.

vocab.money: A region deep inside the brain containing the hippocampus, acting as the critical gateway for turning short-term experiences into permanent long-term memories.

vocab.meaning: A condition where a person can remember their past before an injury, but is completely unable to form any new memories moving forward.
The unconscious muscle memory and motor skills—like riding a bike or typing—that stay intact even when conscious memory is completely destroyed.
Specialized neurons that fire in a precise sequence to stamp our experiences with a sense of duration and order, stitching separate events into a continuous timeline.

quiz.question: What was the primary unintended consequence of William Beecher Scoville's surgery on Patient H.M. in 1953?
options: He lost all memories from his childhood and teenage years.
He became permanently trapped in the present tense, unable to form any new conscious memories.
He lost the ability to control his arms and legs.
He could no longer speak or understand language.
quiz.explanation: Vacuuming out H.M.'s medial temporal lobes permanently deleted his brain's ability to save new long-term memories, freezing him in 1953.

quiz.question: How did Patient H.M. perform on the mirror-drawing star task over multiple days of practice?
options: He got steadily better at it, even though every single day he felt like he was doing it for the very first time.
He never improved because he couldn't remember the instructions.
He refused to do it because it caused him severe physical pain.
He immediately mastered it on the first try because of his childhood memories.
quiz.explanation: H.M.'s motor learning system (procedural memory) allowed him to build physical skill through practice, even though his conscious mind had no memory of ever seeing the star before.

quiz.question: What is the primary function of 'time cells' discovered in the hippocampus?
options: They regulate our sleep cycles and circadian rhythms.
They allow humans to mentally travel back in time to childhood.
They fire in specific sequences to help bridge gaps between moments and construct our experience of passing time.
They stop electrical seizures in patients with severe epilepsy.
quiz.explanation: Time cells act as an internal clockwork, firing sequentially to stitch discrete moments together into a cohesive narrative timeline.
